newsitem.title: UK: Angola's oil rush heralds 1 mln bpd output-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Angola's oil rush heralds 1 mln bpd output-analysts.

text.p: Promising new Angolan offshore discoveries could boost production to close to one million barrels per day (bpd) by 2002, strengthening the war-ravaged country's status as the main West African oil power after Nigeria, analysts say.

But industry watchers familar with Big Oil's giddy rush to West Africa's exploration frontier want to know much more about the commercial viability of the finds before making precise production forecasts.
Angola says it wants to use the potential giant fields uncovered by a fiercely contested exploration race to raise production to one million bpd by the year 2000, from 715,000 bpd now.
Some feel that goal might take two years longer to reach.

"We expect Angola to have one million barrels per day of capacity in the year 2002 and to remain at that level for the foreseeeable future," said Peter Bogin, associate director of Cambridge Energy Research Associates (CERA) in Paris.
"And there is no reason why this production should not come on stream."
Gerald Kepes, managing director of the Upstream Services Group at Petroleum Finance Company in Washington, said good test flow rates did not necessarily translate into big commercial reserves.
"The question is can Angola be a million barrel a day producer and sustain that ratio? They have to confirm that the potential is there, and the numbers are fairly vague so far," Kepes said.

"What we need to see are the results of commercial appraisal activity, and that information is tightly held -- something that's obviously easier to do when you have an offshore play compared to onshore."
"But, yes, these finds are serious," Kepes said, adding that deep water commercial viability demanded a minimum 400 million barrels of reserves.
The excitement about Angola derives mainly from two finds -- 14-2X in the deep water Cabina Block 14 in April 1997 and Girassol 2-A in Block 17 in April 1996.
Partners in 14-2X are Chevron Corp, the operator, Sociedade Nacional de Combusteiveis de Angola (SONANGOL), Agip Angola and Total Angola and Portuguese state oil firm Petrogal Petroleos de Portugal.
"The find is considered to be possibly commercial and a potential giant," wrote Wood Mackenzie analyst Andrew Latham, adding reserves of 500 million barrels were possible.
Partners in Girassol are Elf, the operator, Exxon British Petroleum Plc, Den Norske Stats Oljeselskap ARA (Statoil), Norsk Hydro and Fina Inc.

Latham said total Girassol reserves could be one billion barrels "if subsequent appraisal confirms the potential of the untested features." That would boost Angola's reserves over six billion barrels.
Latham said that assuming 14-2X was not yet on stream he estimated very roughly that total Angolan production could be around 900,000 bpd by the year 2002.

This would be made up of about 600,000 bpd from current wells -- representing a decline from 1997 levels -- plus up to 300,000 bpd from Girassol. If 14-2X could manage 100,000 bpd by then it would bring the total to around one million bpd.
The finds, made possible by high-tech exploration hardware developed in the Gulf of Mexico and North Sea, have touched off aggressive bidding for more unexplored deepwater acreage.

Almost half of all exploration wells in the region are drilled in deep water areas. Activity has been so frenetic -- major oil discoveries in the region have added reserves of about 2.5 billion barrels in recent years -- that drilling units are scarce.

An estimated 15 billion barrels of oil are believed to lie in very deep West African waters. Oil companies are already expected to invest between $40 billion and $60 billion in the region in the next 20 years.
Senior foreign government and oil industry officials have been visiting Angola's decrepit capital Luanda to lobby officials responsible for leasing deepwater blocks.
One company is rumoured to have paid as much as $50 million for the signature fee for an operator's licence.
"In the future there will be even more flies buzzing around the pot," said Elio Dolivo of Petroconsultants in Geneva.

New deep water blocks 21 and 22 south of Luanda were awarded this year respedctively to Australia base Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd and Texaco Inc. Drilling could start within two or three years. Bidding on blocks 23, 24 and 25 are due to open later this year.
Most of Angola's oil production is offshore and has been largely unaffected by the civil war which officially came to an end under a peace treaty signed in 1994.
